title: Transpilation and Qubit Connectivity
summary: Basis gates, coupling maps, SWAP insertion, and why the number of two-qubit gates is the cost of a circuit on hardware.
objectives: Transpile a circuit to a basis-gate set and a coupling map with qiskit.transpile
Explain why a two-qubit gate between non-neighbors costs extra two-qubit gates
Measure the cost of a transpiled circuit with count_ops() and depth()
Reduce the cost by writing a logical circuit that matches the device connectivity
mission: A device has 4 qubits in a line (0 - 1 - 2 - 3) and runs only rz, sx, x and cx. Prepare the GHZ state (|0000⟩ + |1111⟩)/√2 and store in qc the transpiled circuit, with at most 3 two-qubit gates. Every cx in qc must act on neighboring qubits.

prediction.question: On the line 0 - 1 - 2 - 3, with logical qubit i placed on physical qubit i, a circuit holds one cx(0, 3) and nothing else. How many cx does the transpiled circuit have?
options: 4, a single SWAP fixes it, as for qubits two steps apart
10, one SWAP for each of the three links between 0 and 3, plus the gate
7, two SWAPs bring the qubits next to each other, plus the gate itself
prediction.explanation: Qubits 0 and 3 are three links apart, so the state has to travel two links before the two qubits are neighbors: two SWAPs, 6 cx, and then the cx itself, 7. The last link needs no SWAP because the two qubits are already adjacent there. Each extra step of distance costs 3 more cx.

hints: Run the starter code and read count_ops(). Where do the six cx come from when the circuit only has three? Look at which qubit every cx starts from.

Transpiling does not change the algorithm, it only maps it to the device, so the cost depends on the circuit you hand it. Write a GHZ circuit in which every cx acts on a pair of neighbors of the line.

Think of the state spreading along the line: after h(0), qubit 0 can copy its branch onto qubit 1, qubit 1 onto qubit 2, and so on. Then transpile that circuit with the same coupling_map and basis_gates.

messages.ok: The circuit uses only rz, sx, x and cx, every cx acts on neighbors, it prepares the GHZ state, and it has {count} two-qubit gates (depth {depth}).
messages.no_circuit: There is no circuit in qc yet. Store the result of transpile in the variable qc.
messages.wrong_qubits: The device has 4 qubits, but qc has {count}. Build the GHZ circuit on QuantumCircuit(4).
messages.not_basis: qc still contains {gates}, which the device does not run. It usually means transpile was called without basis_gates.
messages.not_adjacent: A two-qubit gate acts on qubits {a} and {b}, which are not neighbors on the line 0 - 1 - 2 - 3. It usually means transpile was called without coupling_map, or the circuit was edited after transpiling.
messages.not_unitary: qc contains a measurement or another non-unitary operation, so its state cannot be compared. Keep only the gates that prepare the state.
messages.wrong_state: qc does not prepare the GHZ state (|0000⟩ + |1111⟩)/√2: the fidelity is {fidelity}. The CNOTs probably copy the 1 branch to the wrong qubits, or the Hadamard gate is missing.
messages.too_many: qc prepares the right state but has {count} two-qubit gates, and the budget is {budget}. The extra ones are SWAPs: change the circuit you transpile so that fewer of them are needed.

challenge.mission: The line of the mission has a convenient end to start from. A device shaped like a T does not: qubits 0, 2 and 4 are ends, and the junction, qubit 1, touches three others. The device now has 5 qubits and the connected pairs are 0-1, 1-2, 1-3 and 3-4. Store in qc the transpiled circuit for the 5-qubit GHZ state (|00000⟩ + |11111⟩)/√2, using only rz, sx, x and cx, with every cx on a connected pair and at most 4 two-qubit gates. A fan-out from qubit 0 needs 7 at optimization level 1, and still 5 at level 3, where the transpiler already looks for a better layout.
hints: Count the cx you need if no SWAP is allowed: every new qubit that joins the state needs a cx that reaches it. Which qubit has the most neighbors?

Grow the state along the edges of the device. After the Hadamard gate, every cx must copy the branch from a qubit that already holds it onto a neighbor that does not, so the order of the cx follows the shape of the T.

Put the Hadamard gate on the junction. Then three cx start from it, one to each neighbor, and a fourth continues from the neighbor that has another neighbor beyond it. Build the coupling map from the four edges, and make it symmetric with make_symmetric() so that a cx can point either way.

messages.ch_ok: The circuit prepares the 5-qubit GHZ state on the T with {count} two-qubit gates, one per new qubit and no SWAP (depth {depth}).
messages.ch_no_circuit: There is no circuit in qc yet. Store the result of transpile in the variable qc.
messages.ch_wrong_qubits: The device has 5 qubits, but qc has {count}. The editor still holds the 4-qubit line of the mission: build the GHZ circuit on QuantumCircuit(5) and the T as the coupling map.
messages.ch_not_basis: qc still contains {gates}, which the device does not run. It usually means transpile was called without basis_gates.
messages.ch_not_connected: A two-qubit gate acts on qubits {a} and {b}, which are not connected on this device (the pairs are 0-1, 1-2, 1-3 and 3-4). Either transpile was called without the T as coupling_map, or the circuit was edited after transpiling.
messages.ch_not_unitary: qc contains a measurement or another non-unitary operation, so its state cannot be compared. Keep only the gates that prepare the state.
messages.ch_wrong_state: qc does not prepare the 5-qubit GHZ state: the fidelity is {fidelity}. A qubit probably never received the branch, or the Hadamard gate is missing.
messages.ch_too_many: qc prepares the right state but has {count} two-qubit gates, and the budget is {budget}. The extra ones are SWAPs: start the state at a qubit that makes every cx a copy onto a neighbor.
